overall_summary: Analysis of 47 deduplicated Shorts reveals a sharp performance divide: extreme planetary superlatives and first-person 'What If You Fell Into...' spatial survival scenarios capture the highest views (up to 1,057) and engagement (up to 3.7% like rate). In contrast, generic psychology facts ('brain memories', 'songs stuck in head') and repetitive regurgitated trivia ('octopus hearts', 'silent space') consistently flatline below 100 views with negligible engagement.

winning_patterns.pattern: First-Person Survival on Extreme Cosmic Anomalies ('What If You Fell Into...')
winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' gained 1,029 views, 38 likes, and 2 comments; 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' reached 972 views; 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' hit 1,031 views and 36 likes.
winning_patterns.action: Leverage immersive, visceral second-person survival framing ('You would not die from heat first...') focused on bizarre, lethal planetary and celestial environments.

winning_patterns.pattern: High-Contrast Planetary Superlatives & Tangible Physical Contradictions
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' reached 1,057 views; 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' hit 981 views and 21 likes; 'Supersonic Rubies' scored 725 views and 25 likes.
winning_patterns.action: Focus hooks on intuitive physical impossibilities (burning ice, raining gems, days longer than years) paired with sensory descriptors.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' achieved between 5 and 53 views across 3 uploads; 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' stalled at 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Cease low-stakes brain trivia unless framed as a high-stakes psychological mystery or biological horror scenario.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Why Space Is Completely Silent' was uploaded 3 times (34, 87, and 220 views); 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' was posted 3 times without traction lift.
weak_patterns.action: Enforce strict deduplication checks and avoid well-worn elementary school facts that lack cinematic tension.

next_video.hook_style: Visceral first-person peril + extreme physical paradox
next_video.concept: What If You Dropped Into the 100-Kilometer-Deep Ocean of Ganymede?
next_video.opening_direction: Start immediately with POV descent through 150 kilometers of solid crust: 'If you fell through Jupiter's moon Ganymede, you wouldn't drown in water—you would be crushed between two layers of ice.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the bottom of the alien ocean isn't rock or seabed, but an exotic form of ice (Ice VI/VII) compressed into rock-hard crystal under pressures that shatter titanium.
next_video.reason: Captures the proven audience demand for first-person cosmic exploration while expanding from exoplanets into deep-space ocean mysteries, avoiding every past covered entity.

Must feature subterranean alien ocean physics and exotic high-pressure ice phases

experiment: Test whether framing deep-space exploration as deep-ocean abyss survival ('oceanic cosmic horror') yields a higher like-to-view conversion (>4%) than hot/rocky exoplanet Shorts.
